claim: Population heterogeneity plays an important role in the spread of epidemics.
source: It is well recognized that population heterogeneity plays an important role in the spread of epidemics.
evidence: This is stated as a well-recognized fact in the introduction, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Individual variations in social activity are often assumed to be persistent (constant in time).
source: While individual variations in social activity are often assumed to be persistent, that is, constant in time, here we discuss the consequences of dynamic heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Integrating stochastic dynamics of social activity into epidemiological models demonstrates the emergence of a new long timescale governing the epidemic.
source: By integrating the stochastic dynamics of social activity into traditional epidemiological models, we demonstrate the emergence of a new long timescale governing the epidemic, in broad agreement with empirical data.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the mathematical model and simulations presented.

claim: The stochastic social activity model captures multiple features of real-life epidemics such as COVID-19, including prolonged plateaus and multiple waves.
source: Our stochastic social activity model captures multiple features of real-life epidemics such as COVID-19, including prolonged plateaus and multiple waves, which are transiently suppressed due to the dynamic nature of social activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by model results and comparison with empirical data.

claim: The interplay between epidemic and social dynamics provides a unifying picture of how a fast-paced epidemic typically will transition to an endemic state.
source: The existence of a long timescale due to the interplay between epidemic and social dynamics provides a unifying picture of how a fast-paced epidemic typically will transition to an endemic state.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: At short timescales, the transmission of infection is highly heterogeneous and characterized by superspreading.
source: It has been well documented that at short timescales the transmission of the infection is highly heterogeneous. That is to say, it is characterized by the phenomenon of superspreading, in which a small fraction of individuals is responsible for a disproportionately large number of secondary infections (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; Galvani and May, 2005; Endo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Persistent population heterogeneity is expected to suppress the herd immunity threshold and reduce the final size of an epidemic.
source: At the same time, according to multiple models, persistent population heterogeneity is expected to suppress the herd immunity threshold (HIT) and reduce the final size of an epidemic (Pastor-Satorras et al., 2015; Bansal et al., 2007; Gomes et al., 2020; Tkachenko et al., 2021; Neipel et al., 2020; Britton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: Locations that have been hardest hit by the first wave of the COVID-19 epidemic have not gained lasting protection against future waves.
source: However, even locations that have been hardest hit by the first wave of the epidemic have not gained a lasting protection against future waves (Faria et al., 2021; Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Plateau-like dynamics characterized by approximately constant incidence rate over a prolonged time is a frequent occurrence in the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: Another puzzling aspect of the COVID-19 pandemic is the frequent occurrence of plateau-like dynamics, characterized by approximately constant incidence rate over a prolonged time (Thurner et al., 2020; Weitz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior observations.

claim: Individuals modify their behavior based on information about the current epidemiological situation.
source: In particular, one plausible mechanism that might be responsible for both suppression of the early waves and plateau-like dynamics is that individuals modify their behavior based on information about the current epidemiological situation (Epstein et al., 2008; Funk et al., 2009; Fenichel et al., 2011; Bauch, 2013; Rizzo et al., 2014; Weitz et al., 2020; Arthur et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research on behavioral adaptation.

claim: Long plateaus might arise because of the underlying structure of social networks.
source: Another possibility is that long plateaus might arise because of the underlying structure of social networks (Thurner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dynamic heterogeneity, even without knowledge-based adaptation of human behavior, leads to a substantial revision of epidemic progression consistent with empirical data for COVID-19.
source: We demonstrate that this type of dynamic heterogeneity, even without knowledge-based adaptation of human behavior (e.g., in response to epidemic-related news) (Epstein et al., 2008; Funk et al., 2009; Fenichel et al., 2011; Bauch, 2013; Rizzo et al., 2014; Weitz et al., 2020; Arthur et al., 2021), leads to a substantial revision of the epidemic progression, consistent with empirical data for the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by model results and data comparison.

claim: Population heterogeneity is a dynamic property that roams across multiple timescales.
source: In a recent study (Tkachenko et al., 2021), we have pointed out that population heterogeneity is a dynamic property that roams across multiple timescales.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Strong short-term overdispersion of individual infectivity manifests itself in the statistics of superspreading events.
source: A strong short-term overdispersion of the individual infectivity manifests itself in the statistics of superspreading events.
evidence: This is stated as an established relationship in the field.

claim: Long-term heterogeneity leads to a reduction of the herd immunity threshold compared to that predicted by classical homogeneous models.
source: In particular, it is this long-term heterogeneity that leads to a reduction of the HIT compared to that predicted by classical homogeneous models (Gomes et al., 2020; Tkachenko et al., 2021; Neipel et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2021; Britton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The suppression of early waves of the COVID-19 epidemic without active mitigation does not signal achievement of long-term herd immunity.
source: Due to this type of dynamic heterogeneity, the suppression of early waves of the COVID-19 epidemic, even without active mitigation, does not signal achievement of long-term herd immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: Suppression of early epidemic waves is associated with transient collective immunity (TCI), a fragile state that degrades over time as individuals change their social activity patterns.
source: Instead, as argued in Tkachenko et al., 2021, this suppression is associated with transient collective immunity (TCI), a fragile state that degrades over time as individuals change their social activity patterns.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The first wave is generally followed either by secondary waves or by long plateaus characterized by a nearly constant incidence rate.
source: In this work, we present a stochastic social activity (SSA) model explicitly incorporating time-dependent heterogeneity and demonstrate that the first wave is generally followed either by secondary waves or by long plateaus characterized by a nearly constant incidence rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by model results.

claim: Long plateaus and multiwave epidemic dynamics have been commonly observed in the context of COVID-19.
source: In the context of COVID-19, both long plateaus and multiwave epidemic dynamics have been commonly observed.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation.

claim: The number of daily infections during the plateau regime and individual wave trajectories are robust properties of the epidemic that depend on the current level of mitigation, degree of heterogeneity, and temporal correlations of individual social activity.
source: According to our analysis, the number of daily infections during the plateau regime, as well as the individual wave trajectories, are robust properties of the epidemic and depend on the current level of mitigation, degree of heterogeneity, and temporal correlations of individual social activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: Once plateau-like dynamics is established, the epidemic gradually evolves towards the long-term herd immunity threshold determined by persistent population heterogeneity.
source: Our work implies that, once plateau-like dynamics is established, the epidemic gradually evolves towards the long-term HIT determined by persistent population heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: Reaching the long-term herd immunity threshold may stretch over a surprisingly long time, from months to years.
source: However, reaching that state may stretch over a surprisingly long time, from months to years.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: On long timescales, both waning of individual biological immunity and mutations of the pathogen become valid concerns and would ultimately result in a permanent endemic state of the infection.
source: On these long timescales, both waning of individual biological immunity and mutations of the pathogen become valid concerns and would ultimately result in a permanent endemic state of the infection.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known biological processes.

claim: Endemic behavior is a well-known property of most classical epidemiological models.
source: Such endemic behavior is a well-known property of most classical epidemiological models (Keeling and Rohani, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a textbook on epidemiological modeling.

claim: The emergence of the endemic state for a newly introduced pathogen is far from being completely understood.
source: However, the emergence of the endemic state for a newly introduced pathogen is far from being completely understood (Wolfe et al., 2007; Engering et al., 2019; Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani, 2001a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most epidemiological models would typically predict complete extinction of a pathogen following the first wave of the epidemic, well before the pool of susceptible population would be replenished.
source: Indeed, most epidemiological models would typically predict complete extinction of a pathogen following the first wave of the epidemic, well before the pool of susceptible population would be replenished.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of classical models.

claim: A commonly accepted explanation for the onset of endemic behavior involves geographic heterogeneity where the pathogen may survive in other geographic locations until returning to a hard-hit area with a depleted susceptible pool.
source: A commonly accepted, though mostly qualitative, explanation for the onset of endemic behavior of such diseases as measles, seasonal cold, etc., involves geographic heterogeneity: the pathogen may survive in other geographic locations until returning to a hard-hit area with a depleted susceptible pool (Wolfe et al., 2007; Engering et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The theory provides a simple and general mechanism that prevents an overshoot of the epidemic dynamics and thus naturally and generically leads to the endemic fixed point.
source: In contrast, our theory provides a simple and general mechanism that prevents an overshoot of the epidemic dynamics and thus naturally and generically leads to the endemic fixed point.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the model analysis.

claim: The importance of temporal effects has long been recognized in the context of network-based epidemiological models.
source: The importance of temporal effects has long been recognized in the context of network-based epidemiological models (Starnini et al., 2017; Volz and Meyers, 2007; Bansal et al., 2010; Read et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Social activity determines both the individual susceptibility to infection as well as the ability to infect others.
source: This quantity determines both the individual susceptibility to infection as well as the ability to infect others.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: Virtual interactions by means of e-mail, social media, and mobile communications are commonly used as proxies for studies of interpersonal contacts.
source: In addition, virtual interactions by means of e-mail, social media, and mobile communications are commonly used as proxies for studies of interpersonal contacts (Rybski et al., 2009; Barabási, 2005; Saramäki and Moro, 2015; Nielsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The analysis of various communication networks reveals a cutoff time, beyond which the level of activity reverts to its long-term average.
source: While individuals demonstrate bursts of activity across multiple timescales, the analysis of various communication networks reveals a cutoff time, beyond which the level of activity reverts to its long-term average (Vazquez et al., 2007; Karsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mean-reversion time constant may range from days to months, depending on the context of the study.
source: Note that this average may still exhibit person-to-person variations corresponding to persistent heterogeneity of the population. The mean-reversion time constant may range from days to months, depending on the context of the study (Vazquez et al., 2007; Karsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term epidemic dynamics is fueled by replenishment of the susceptible population due to changes in the level of individual social activity from low to high.
source: Qualitatively it leads to long-term epidemic dynamics fueled by replenishment of the susceptible population due to changes in the level of individual social activity from low to high.
evidence: This is a qualitative conclusion from the model.

claim: Variations in activity on timescales shorter than the mean generation interval may be safely ignored from the point of view of epidemic dynamics.
source: Note that from the point of view of the epidemic dynamics, variations in activity on timescales shorter than the mean generation interval may be safely ignored.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model.

claim: The stochastic process is well known in mathematical finance as the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) model.
source: This stochastic process is well known in mathematical finance as the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) model (Cox et al., 1985) and has been studied in probability theory since the 1950s (Feller, 1951).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in mathematics and finance.

claim: The major properties of the CIR model are (i) reversion to the mean and (ii) non-negativity of ai at all times.
source: The major properties of this model are (i) reversion to the mean and (ii) non-negativity of ai at all times, both of which are natural for social activity.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the CIR model.

claim: The steady-state solution of the CIR model is characterized by gamma-distributed ai.
source: Furthermore, the steady-state solution of this model is characterized by gamma-distributed ai.
evidence: This is a known mathematical property of the CIR model.

claim: The gamma distribution of ai is consistent with the empirical statistics of short-term overdispersion of disease transmission manifesting itself in superspreading events.
source: This is consistent with the empirical statistics of short-term overdispersion of disease transmission manifesting itself in superspreading events (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; Endo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The short-term overdispersion has both stochastic and persistent contributions.
source: This short-term overdispersion has both stochastic and persistent contributions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the sources of overdispersion.

claim: The theory described by Equations 4, 5, 6 is in excellent agreement with simulations of an agent-based model.
source: As demonstrated below, the theory described by Equation 4, Equation 5, Equation 6 is in excellent agreement with simulations of an agent-based model (ABM) in which social activities of 1 million agents undergo stochastic evolution described by Equation 1 (compare solid lines with shaded areas in Figure 3 and Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model predictions with ABM simulations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In the case of dynamic heterogeneity, the epidemic is transiently suppressed at a level that is below even the heterogeneous HIT.
source: In the case of dynamic heterogeneity (green), described by Equation 4; Equation 5; Equation 6, the epidemic is transiently suppressed at a level that is below even the heterogeneous HIT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and explained in the text.

claim: As the TCI state degrades, the daily incidence rate develops an extended plateau.
source: Figure 3b illustrates that as the TCI state degrades, the daily incidence rate develops an extended plateau on the green curve.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The existence of the universal attractor is apparent in Figure 4, where two scenarios with different mitigation strategies eventually converge to the same trajectory.
source: The existence of the universal attractor is apparent in Figure 4, where we compare two scenarios with different mitigation strategies applied at early stages of the epidemic.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Differences in initial mitigation have not had any significant effect on the epidemic in the long run.
source: As predicted, this difference in mitigation has not had any significant effect on the epidemic in the long run: these two trajectories eventually converged towards the universal attractor.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Early mitigation allows the peak of the infection to be suppressed, potentially reducing stress on the healthcare system.
source: However, early mitigation allows the peak of the infection to be suppressed, potentially reducing stress on the healthcare system.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and explained in the text.

claim: Delayed mitigation gives rise to a sizable second wave.
source: A delayed mitigation gives rise to a sizable second wave.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The universal attractor leads to a fixed point corresponding to the endemic state.
source: The analysis of our equations, modified in this way, shows that the universal attractor leads to a fixed point corresponding to the endemic state.
evidence: This is a mathematical result from the modified model.

claim: A similar endemic steady state exists in most classical epidemic models.
source: A similar endemic steady state exists in most classical epidemic models (see Keeling and Rohani, 2011 and references therein).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a textbook.

claim: In classical models, epidemic dynamics would not normally lead to the endemic point due to overshoot.
source: However, in those cases, epidemic dynamics would not normally lead to that point due to overshoot.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of classical models.

claim: Classical models typically predict a complete extinction of the disease when the prevalence drops below one infected individual.
source: Instead, these models typically predict a complete extinction of the disease when the prevalence drops below one infected individual.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of classical models.

claim: When time-dependent heterogeneity is included, the mechanism leads to an endemic state rather than pathogen extinction, even in closed and reasonably small populations.
source: That is not the case when time-dependent heterogeneity is included. Furthermore, in contrast to classical models, even in closed and reasonably small populations our mechanism would lead to an endemic state rather than pathogen extinction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: The model is able to describe seasonal dynamics as well as the transition towards it for a new pathogen.
source: Our model is able to describe this seasonal dynamics as well as the transition towards it for a new pathogen (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: The model captures important qualitative features of seasonal waves of real pathogens, including sharp peaks followed by prolonged relaxation and the possibility of multi-annual cycles due to parametric resonance.
source: It captures the important qualitative features of seasonal waves of real pathogens, for example, the three endemic coronavirus families studied in Neher et al., 2020. They are (i) sharp peaks followed by a prolonged relaxation towards the annual minimum and (ii) a possibility of multi-annual cycles due to parametric resonance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis and comparison with real pathogens.

claim: In the case of persistent heterogeneity without temporal variations of social activity, the infection becomes extinct following the initial wave of the epidemic.
source: In the case of persistent heterogeneity without temporal variations of social activity (brown solid line), the infection becomes extinct following the initial wave of the epidemic.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dynamic heterogeneity leads to an endemic state with strong seasonal oscillations.
source: In contrast, dynamic heterogeneity leads to an endemic state with strong seasonal oscillations (green line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: A combination of spiral dynamics with a slow drift towards the endemic state gives rise to the overall trajectory shown in Figure 5.
source: A combination of this spiral dynamics with a slow drift towards the endemic state gives rise to the overall trajectory shown as the solid green line in the inset to Figure 5.
evidence: This is shown in the inset to Figure 5.

claim: The periodic seasonal forcing generates a limit cycle about the endemic point.
source: The periodic seasonal forcing generates a limit cycle about the endemic point (small green ellipse around the red point).
evidence: This is shown in the inset to Figure 5.

claim: Any abrupt increase of the effective reproduction number would shift the endemic fixed point up along the universal attractor and trigger a spiral-like relaxation manifesting as a new wave of the epidemic.
source: More generally, any abrupt increase of the effective reproduction number, for example, due to a relaxed mitigation, seasonal changes, etc., would shift the endemic fixed point up along the universal attractor. According to Equation 4; Equation 5; Equation 6 this will once again trigger a spiral-like relaxation. It will manifest itself as a new wave of the epidemic, such as the secondary waves in Figure 4b.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis and illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: Multiple factors are known to affect epidemic dynamics: government-imposed mitigation, knowledge-based adaptation of social behavior, seasonal forces, vaccinations, emergence of new variants, etc.
source: In addition to stochastic changes in social activity, multiple other factors are known to affect the epidemic dynamics: government-imposed mitigation, knowledge-based adaptation of social behavior, seasonal forces, vaccinations, emergence of new variants, etc.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A principled way of integrating the effects of mitigation and knowledge-based adaptation is to use average mobility data.
source: A principled way of integrating the effects of mitigation and knowledge-based adaptation is to use average mobility data.
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors.

claim: Mobility data capture population-wide trends in social activity while averaging out individual-level stochasticity.
source: By their nature, these data capture population-wide trends in social activity, while averaging out individual-level stochasticity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of mobility data.

claim: Google Mobility Data for retail and recreation in four major regions of the USA exhibit pronounced effects of government-imposed mitigation and knowledge-based adaptation during spring-early summer of 2020.
source: In Figure 6, we show historic Google Mobility Data for retail and recreation in four major regions of the USA: Northeast, Midwest, South, and West (China Data Lab Dataverse, 2021). These data exhibit pronounced effects of government-imposed mitigation and knowledge-based adaptation of the population during spring-early summer of 2020.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and based on Google Mobility Data.

claim: There is only modest and slow variation in mobility from mid-July 2020 through mid-February 2021 across all four US regions.
source: In contrast, there is only a modest and slow variation in the mobility from mid-July 2020 through mid-February 2021 (shaded area) across all four regions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The variation in mobility from mid-July 2020 through mid-February 2021 is generally consistent with regular seasonal effects and lacks signs of drastic and fast changes similar to those observed in the early stages of the epidemic.
source: This variation is generally consistent with regular seasonal effects and lacks any signs of the drastic and fast changes similar to those observed in the early stages of the epidemic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The time interval from mid-July 2020 through mid-February 2021 is optimal for testing the predictions of the theory without embarking on calibration of a full-scale active mitigation model.
source: Hence, this time interval is optimal for testing the predictions of our theory without embarking on calibration of a full-scale active mitigation model.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the suitability of this time period for model testing.

claim: The time window from mid-July 2020 through mid-February 2021 excludes the effects of mass vaccinations and the introduction of COVID-19 variants of concern.
source: Furthermore, this time window also excludes the effects of mass vaccinations and the introduction of COVID-19 variants of concern (CDC, 2021), which became relevant after February/March 2021.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to CDC data.

claim: The progression of the COVID-19 epidemic from July 2020 until February 2021 in all four US regions can be well described by the theory.
source: Below we present a proof-of-principle demonstration that the progression of the COVID-19 epidemic from July 2020 until February 2021 in all four regions can indeed be well described by our theory.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study to be demonstrated.

claim: The IFR value of 0.5% was estimated by comparing reported COVID-related deaths in the USA to two independent seroprevalence surveys.
source: This IFR value was estimated by comparing reported COVID-related deaths in the USA to two independent seroprevalence surveys (Anand et al., 2020; Angulo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to seroprevalence studies.

claim: According to the model, the wave in each of the US regions was triggered by the seasonal changes in transmission.
source: Thus, this wave in each of the regions was triggered by the seasonal changes in transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: According to the model, the wave was stabilized in mid-winter due to the population reaching the TCI state.
source: According to our model, this wave was stabilized in mid-winter due to the population reaching the TCI state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model analysis.

claim: There is good agreement between the model and the empirical data for all four US regions.
source: There is a good agreement between our model and the empirical data for all four regions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Fitting the empirical data in the Midwest region up to November 15, 2020, and projecting the epidemic dynamics beyond that date with the SSA model gives a very good prediction of the overall seasonal wave.
source: To do that, the empirical data in Midwest region have been fitted up to November 15, 2020, and the epidemic dynamics beyond that date has been projected by our SSA model. As shown in Figure 8, this procedure gives a very good prediction of the overall seasonal wave, based only on its onset behavior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: Use of the traditional SIR model leads to an almost threefold overestimate of the height of the peak, with predicted timing about a month later than is observed.
source: In contrast, use of the traditional SIR model leads to an almost threefold overestimate of the height of the peak, with predicted timing about a month later than is observed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: The timing of the peak of the wave in all four US regions is in closer agreement with the SSA model than the SIR model.
source: The timing of the peak of the wave in all four regions is in closer agreement with the SSA model than the SIR model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison shown in Figure 8 and Appendix 5—figure 2.

claim: The height of the peak in all four US regions is in closer agreement with the SSA model than the SIR model, except for the South region where it is somewhere in between the predictions of these two models.
source: The same is true for the height of the peak except for the South region, where it is somewhere in between the predictions of these two models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison shown in Figure 8 and Appendix 5—figure 2.

claim: A new theory integrating the stochastic dynamics of individual social activity into traditional epidemiological models has been proposed.
source: In conclusion, we have proposed a new theory integrating the stochastic dynamics of individual social activity into traditional epidemiological models.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: The SSA model describes the 'zero intelligence' limit in which there is no feedback from the epidemic dynamics to social activity.
source: Our SSA model describes the so-called 'zero intelligence' limit in which there is no feedback from the epidemic dynamics to social activity, for example, mediated by the news.
evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claim: The SSA approach is complementary to knowledge-based models.
source: Hence, our approach is complementary to knowledge-based models of Epstein et al., 2008; Funk et al., 2009; Fenichel et al., 2011; Bauch, 2013; Rizzo et al., 2014; Weitz et al., 2020; Arthur et al., 2021.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship of this work to prior research.

claim: The SSA in the approach is described by the CIR model which captures three important properties: non-negativity of activity, reversion towards long-term average, and gamma-distributed short-term overdispersion.
source: The SSA in our approach is described by the CIR model (Cox et al., 1985), which captures the following important properties: (i) the activity cannot be negative; (ii) for any given individual, it reverses towards its long-term average value; and (iii) it exhibits gamma-distributed short-term overdispersion (aka superspreading) (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; Endo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the model properties.

claim: The overall epidemic dynamics featuring heterogeneous time-varying social activity was mapped onto a system of three differential equations, two of which generalize the traditional SIR model.
source: We mapped the overall epidemic dynamics featuring heterogeneous time-varying social activity onto a system of three differential equations, two of which generalize the traditional SIR model.
evidence: This is a summary of the mathematical approach.

claim: The emergent timescale might be of relevance to public health measures as it describes when the epidemic is reaching a sustainable plateau and for how long this plateau is expected to last.
source: This emergent timescale might be of relevance to public health measures as it describes when the epidemic is reaching a sustainable plateau and for how long this plateau is expected to last.
evidence: This is a discussion of the practical implications of the findings.

claim: The long-term dynamics of the model is in striking contrast to traditional epidemiological models, generally characterized by a large overshoot above the HIT leading to a likely extinction of new pathogens.
source: The long-term dynamics of our model is in striking contrast to traditional epidemiological models, generally characterized by a large overshoot above the HIT leading to a likely extinction of new pathogens.
evidence: This is a comparison of the model results with traditional models.

claim: The theory provides a plausible explanation for the long plateaus observed in real-life epidemics such as COVID-19.
source: Our theory provides a plausible explanation for the long plateaus observed in real-life epidemics such as COVID-19.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: The theory provides a qualitative description of transient suppression of individual epidemic waves well below the HIT.
source: It also provides a qualitative description of transient suppression of individual epidemic waves well below the HIT (Tkachenko et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding with a citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanism explains how the winter 2020/21 waves of the COVID-19 epidemic in the USA were suppressed in the absence of a noticeable reduction in the population mobility.
source: In particular, this mechanism explains how the winter 2020/21 waves of the COVID-19 epidemic in the USA were suppressed in the absence of a noticeable reduction in the population mobility.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.
